newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Family eroding in EU, Eurostat says.
newsitem.headline: Family eroding in EU, Eurostat says.

text.p: The traditional family in the European Union is being eroded, with one person in 10 living alone and 5.62 million children living with only one parent, the EU's statistical office Eurostat said on Wednesday.

Unveiling new figures covering 12 of the EU member states, Eurostat said that although the legal family union between man and woman was still the norm -- with 72 percent living in one -- it was an institution in decline.

The figures showed a wide gulf between the southern Mediterranean states like Greece and Spain, where the family unit predominates, and the northern countries like Denmark, the Netherlands and Germany where it is being discarded.
"...In the Mediterranean countries and Ireland, children tend to stay with parents until starting new families themselves, usually upon marriage," the Luxembourg-based agency said in a statement.
"In the north, the transition from parental home to forming a new family is less straightforward, marked by spells of living alone and in unmarried couples," it added.
The statistics do not cover the EU's three latest members Austria, Finland and Sweden.
In Denmark, the figures show, nearly 22 percent of people live alone, while the figure is around 14 percent in Germany and the Netherlands.
Figures for the Mediterranean and Ireland, however, paint a different picture.
In Greece only 6.7 percent live alone and the figure is 7.5 percent in Italy, 6.6 percent in Ireland, 4.4 percent in Portugal and 4.0 percent in Spain .

The report shows that eight percent of the EU's 72 million children under 16 live in single parent families with the proportion ranging from under four percent in Greece and Spain to over 14 percent in Denmark and 15 percent in Britain.
The number of couples cohabiting is also growing, with differences according to region and age, it says.

Ninety percent of EU couples are married. Nearly all couples in the Meditteranean countries are legally married, but only 76 percent have tied the knot in Denmark and 87 percent in France, the statisics show.

"The phenomenon of cohabitation is certainly an example of changing customs, particularly widespread among the young, and EU-wide this accounts for around 28 percent of the under 30s but drops to 6.7 percent for those aged 30-40 and to two percent for those 45 plus," it said.
Patterns for the under 30s vary between countries, ranging from 70 percent in Denmark to 9.7 percent in Greece and Portugal, it said.
The figures show that while couples with children still predominate, more and more couples are living without children, ranging from eight percent in Ireland to 25.9 percent in Denmark.
Ireland has the biggest families by far, with half the population living in families of five or more, the figures show.
